strengths: The paper introduces a genuinely novel and well-motivated construction: vector diffusion wavelets built from local SVD-based frames (inspired by vector diffusion maps), extending geometric scattering to vector-valued node features on geometric graphs without assuming a manifold structure.

The theoretical contribution is solid and self-contained: the frame bound (Theorem 3.1), wavelet equivariance (Theorem 3.2), and scattering equivariance (Theorem 3.3) are proved in full in the appendix, and the sign-ambiguity issue in the SVD-based local frames is identified and handled with a concrete technique (Appendix C).

The empirical evaluation is transparent: five-fold CV, validation vs. rotated-test split, parameter counts, and per-epoch training/inference runtimes are all reported, and an ablation (non-equivariant ESc-GNN) cleanly isolates the benefit of equivariance.

Reproducibility is well supported: code availability is stated, EGNN/TFN baselines are adapted from a public repo, and Appendix E provides extensive hyperparameter, data-construction, and complexity details.

The paper is honest about where its implementation deviates from the theory (generalized InfoGain wavelets, no nonlinearity in the scattering coefficients, additional Dirac signals) and asserts these can be adapted to the theory.

The experiments convincingly demonstrate the claimed phenomenon: non-equivariant baselines fail badly under rotation while ESc-GNN remains stable, at a small fraction of the parameter count of EGNN/TFN.
weaknesses: The experimental evidence is limited to synthetic ellipsoid point-cloud tasks. No standard real-world equivariant benchmarks (e.g., QM9, MD17, N-Body, molecular property prediction) are included, so claims of practical usefulness beyond controlled settings remain unverified.

The headline parameter-efficiency comparison is somewhat favorable by construction: TFN is a very old and parameter-heavy baseline (29M parameters, trained on 4 GPUs), and only EGNN and TFN represent the modern equivariant literature; stronger but more efficient equivariant baselines (e.g., GVP-GNN, ESCNN-style models, PaiNN) are absent.

The abstract claims SE(3)-equivariance, but the theorems only establish SO(d) equivariance; translation equivariance is likely to hold by construction (all quantities are relative to neighbors), but it is never stated or proved, so the abstract slightly overclaims.

The equivariance theorems are relatively incremental: they follow fairly directly from the parallel-transport structure of the O_{i,j} matrices (Lemma A.2/B.2) and an existing nonexpansive frame result (Proposition B.1 of Perlmutter et al., 2023), so the theoretical novelty is moderate relative to the framing.

There is a gap between the exposition and the actual experimental system (InfoGain-selected non-dyadic scales, no activation in the scattering coefficients, Dirac probes); the claim that the theory 'may be readily adapted' is asserted but not demonstrated, which weakens the theory-to-practice link.

Several assumptions limiting applicability are treated lightly: distinct singular values for every node, node degrees forced to at least d by adding edges, and the test-set-only rotation protocol, which is a somewhat artificial way to demonstrate equivariance.

The manuscript contains numerous typos and minor errors (e.g., 'singal', 'Guassian', 'otherwiswe', 'rationally invariant' for 'rotationally invariant', an incomplete URL in Appendix E), which slightly detract from presentation quality.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated contribution: the paper extends the geometric scattering transform to vector-valued signals on geometric graphs, a genuine gap in the scattering/GDL literature (prior work did not handle vector-valued node features or non-manifold geometric graphs).

Solid theoretical core: Theorems 3.1–3.3 (frame bounds, wavelet equivariance, scattering equivariance) are proven carefully in the appendices, including the nontrivial details of Lemma A.2 (block form of Q^m via parallel transport matrices O_{i,j}) and the sign-ambiguity resolution in Appendix C. The theory is supported by illustrative Figures 1–2.

The method is attractive practically: parameter efficiency (roughly 5–500x fewer parameters than EGNN/TFN) with comparable performance on the tested tasks, plus a detailed complexity analysis (Appendix D.1) and runtime tables (Tables 3–4).
Good reproducibility: the codebase is stated to be available, hyperparameters, CV procedure, baseline configurations, and even GPU details are reported in detail (Appendix E).
Honest handling of the equivariant-vs-non-equivariant ablation makes the practical importance of equivariance tangible (validation vs. rotated-test MSE gap).
weaknesses: Experimental validation is limited to small synthetic data (512 ellipsoid point clouds of 128 points). No real-world benchmarks (e.g., QM9, MD17, ESOL, N-Body dynamics) are tested, which substantially weakens the central empirical claim that the method achieves 'comparable performance to other equivariant GNNs' in general. The rotated-test-set design (rotating only test data by 90 degrees) demonstrates equivariance almost by construction rather than testing real distribution shift.

A mismatch between abstract and theory: the abstract claims SE(3)-equivariance, but only SO(d) rotational equivariance is proven. Translation equivariance/invariance is never formally analyzed despite positions being the motivating vector feature; the local bases U_i are translation-invariant, but this should be stated and proven.

The implemented model deviates from the theoretically analyzed one: generalized (InfoGain-selected) rather than dyadic wavelets, no nonlinearity in the scattering coefficients, and Dirac features are added. The authors assert that 'all of our theoretical guarantees may be readily adapted,' but this is not demonstrated, so the theory does not strictly certify the model that is evaluated.

Baseline comparability concerns: ESc-GNN uses 59,779 parameters versus 14,481 for its own non-equivariant ablation and 15,335 for LEGS, so parameter-matched comparisons are not provided; also TFN is restricted to l=2 and EGNN layer counts are tuned, but tuning budgets across methods are not fully equalized.

Several assumptions deserve more scrutiny: distinct singular values of B_i (degenerate cases are waved away), n_i >= d enforced by modifying the graph (which affects Q and its equivariance analysis), and the sign-alignment heuristic's effect under global rotations could have been discussed more rigorously.

Presentation issues: numerous typos ('Guassian', 'singal', 'otherwiswe', 'rationally invariant' where rotational invariance is meant, 'The case case'), and a truncated URL for the codebase in Appendix E ('which is available at For the EGNN...') slightly undermines the reproducibility claim.

strengths: The core contribution—extending diffusion wavelets to vector-valued (tangent-bundle-like) features via a vector diffusion matrix Q inspired by vector diffusion maps—is well motivated and fills a genuine gap between scalar diffusion-wavelet GNNs and tangent-bundle/sheaf methods.

The theoretical contribution is complete and carefully executed: frame bounds (Thm 3.1), wavelet equivariance (Thm 3.2), and scattering equivariance (Thm 3.3) are all proven in full, including nontrivial details such as the SVD sign-ambiguity resolution (Appendix C) and the connection to existing frame theory via Proposition B.1.

Experiments span three progressively complex settings (synthetic ellipsoids, wind-field reconstruction, neural recordings), with appropriate equivariant and non-equivariant baselines, rotated test sets that directly test the claimed symmetry, cross-validation, runtime comparisons, and honest reporting (e.g., noting the MARBLE difference is not statistically significant).

Strong parameter and runtime efficiency: VDW-GNN matches or beats EGNN/TFN/DD-TNN with orders of magnitude fewer parameters (e.g., ~60K vs ~30M for TFN on ellipsoids), and the sparse, eigendecomposition-free construction is practical and well analyzed in Appendix D.
Very good reproducibility: code availability, full hyperparameter tables, preprocessing details, early-stopping procedures, and baseline adaptation details in Appendices E–G.
weaknesses: The theory, while correct and complete, is largely a structured extension of existing scalar diffusion-wavelet frame results (Perlmutter et al., 2023; Gama et al., 2018) to a Kronecker-type operator; the proofs (Lemmas A.1–A.3) are relatively elementary inductions, limiting theoretical novelty.

Empirical improvements over the strongest baselines are modest: on the neural task the gain over MARBLE is not significant (admitted by the authors), and on the wind task EGNN achieves better rotated MSE. The headline advantages are mainly parameter count and speed rather than accuracy.

The equivariance theory assumes rotations do not change graph connectivity (A = Ā) and that local SVD singular values are non-degenerate; neither assumption is analyzed for robustness in practice (e.g., k-NN graphs built from rotated point clouds can in principle change edges, and near-degenerate singular values make local frames unstable).

There are theory–practice gaps: the experiments use non-dyadic InfoGain-selected scales, no activation in scattering coefficients, and Dirac auxiliary signals (Appendix E.1); the authors assert the guarantees 'readily adapt,' but no formal statement is given for the exact deployed model.
Minor presentation issues: typos ('Guassian kernel', 'in term of', 'represtenta-tion'), and the code-availability footnote in Section 4 appears incomplete/empty in the manuscript.

The custom experimental protocol choices (rotation only applied to the test set in the ellipsoids task; directed modified k-NN graph and masked-node handling in the wind task) are reasonable but introduce some comparability concerns with baselines, and the datasets are relatively small-scale.

strengths: The theoretical portion is technically sound and clearly presented. The frame bound (Theorem 3.1) and the SO(D)-equivariance results (Theorems 3.2, 3.3) are proven in detail in the appendix, and the key structural lemma (Lemma A.2, that Q^m[i,j] = P^m[i,j]O_{i,j}) is a clean observation that makes the proofs straightforward and verifiable.

The paper is well-positioned relative to prior work: the connection to vector diffusion maps (Singer & Wu, 2012) and the connection Laplacian perspective (Battiloro et al., 2024) is explicitly discussed, and computational aspects (sparse block structure of Q, cached preprocessing, complexity analysis in Appendix D) are treated carefully.

Experiments cover three progressively realistic settings (synthetic ellipsoids, wind field reconstruction, neural recordings) with appropriate baselines including non-equivariant ablations of the authors' own model, which convincingly demonstrates the practical value of the equivariance property on rotated test sets.
The method is very parameter-efficient compared to equivariant baselines (e.g., 57K parameters vs. ~29M for TFN), and code is stated to be available, supporting reproducibility.

The inductive evaluation protocol for the neural data experiment (withholding entire trials rather than transductive node holdout) is a more stringent test than the original MARBLE setup and is a methodologically fair design choice.
weaknesses: Limited originality. The core construction is essentially the natural combination of two well-known ingredients: vector diffusion maps / the connection Laplacian discretization (Singer & Wu, 2012; Battiloro et al., 2024) and classical diffusion wavelets (Coifman & Maggioni, 2006). The authors themselves acknowledge DD-TNN uses the same local-SVD matrices O_{i,j} to build a sheaf/connection Laplacian; the delta over that work is mainly replacing spectral convolutions with wavelet/scattering-style filters, which is a known recipe from the scalar case.

The theoretical results, while correct, are largely expected consequences of the block structure of Q via unitary equivalence with Q' = P ⊗ I (Theorem 3.1) and the equivariance of the local frames (Lemma A.3). The contribution is a verification of desirable properties rather than new understanding that is surprising or deep.

Empirical evidence is thin and mixed. The headline neural-data result (66% vs. MARBLE's 65%) is acknowledged by the authors to be statistically non-significant under a two-sided Wilcoxon test, so the strongest real-world claim is essentially parity with an existing method. The wind-field experiment uses a subsample of only 2000 nodes from a single day of data, which limits generality.

Experimental fairness concerns. In the neural experiment, the proposed model uses a custom supervised contrastive loss with a bespoke hard-negatives sampling module, and preprocessing differs from the baselines (e.g., PCA is deliberately not applied 'for any model' per the authors' finding). These design choices conflate the benefit of the VDW representation with the benefit of the tuned objective, weakening attribution of the gains to the wavelet construction.

There is a gap between theory and implementation. The equivariance guarantees apply to the wavelets and scattering coefficients with activations commuting with rotations, but the actual VDW-GNN architecture (MLP mixing layers, gating functions, invariant extraction, prediction heads) has no formal equivariance proof in the paper; the implementation also departs from the theory (non-dyadic InfoGain-selected scales, no nonlinearity in the scattering coefficients, added Dirac features). The authors note the guarantees 'may be readily adapted,' but this is not demonstrated.

The method carries practical restrictions not fully probed: Q requires an SVD per node with the assumption of distinct singular values (degenerate/local-flat geometries may violate this), and construction costs O((n+m)D^3), which could be prohibitive for high ambient dimension; no scaling or stress experiments are reported.

Several presentation issues remain: a typo in the statement of Theorem 3.2 (mixing Φ̃_J and Φ̃_j), an incomplete sentence at the end of Section 3 on computational efficiency, and the code link on page 5 is not rendered.

strengths: The core construction of vector diffusion wavelets via a vector diffusion matrix Q (built from local SVD frames and parallel-transport matrices O_{i,j}) is clean, well-motivated, and connects naturally to vector diffusion maps (Singer & Wu, 2012) and the connection Laplacian.

The theoretical results are properly proven: frame bounds (Theorem 3.1) via a Kronecker-product reduction to the scalar case, and rotational equivariance of the powered diffusion matrix, wavelets, and scattering coefficients (Theorems 3.2-3.3), with complete proofs and a careful treatment of the SVD sign-ambiguity issue (Appendix C). The assumptions (σ commutes with rotations, connectivity preserved under rotation) are stated honestly and discussed.

Experiments span three progressively complex settings (synthetic ellipsoids, real wind fields, neural recordings) with relevant baselines including equivariant GNNs (EGNN, TFN), a scattering GNN (LEGS), message-passing baselines, DD-TNN, MARBLE, CEBRA, and LFADS. The rotated-test-set protocol is a sensible way to probe equivariance in practice, and the method consistently achieves strong results with a fraction of the parameter count (e.g., 59,779 params vs. 29.7M for TFN).
The wind-field experiment substantially outperforms DD-TNN (12.76 vs 2.75 MSE), the closest prior method designed for tangent-bundle features, which is a meaningful head-to-head result.

Computational complexity is analyzed (Appendix D), sparse implementation is described, and the neural-data experiment adopts a more stringent inductive protocol than the original transductive MARBLE setup, which the authors appropriately frame as a contribution of the evaluation design rather than overclaiming significance (they report the Wilcoxon test showing non-significance vs. MARBLE).
weaknesses: Originality is modest: the work is essentially a direct transplant of dyadic diffusion wavelets onto the vector diffusion matrix of Singer & Wu (2012), and DD-TNN (Battiloro et al., 2024) already constructs a sheaf/connection Laplacian from the same local-SVD machinery. The main theorems are close analogs of known scalar results and follow fairly directly from Lemma A.2 (Q^m[i,j] = P^m[i,j] O_{i,j}), so the theoretical contribution is incremental rather than revealing new structure.

Experimental scale is limited: the wind task uses a single day of data subsampled to 2000 measurements; the synthetic tasks are small (128-point ellipsoids). There is no empirical scalability demonstration despite the efficiency claims, and no ablations on the frame bounds, the number of scales, or the effect of the (assumed-away) singular value multiplicity condition, which may fail on symmetric geometries in practice.

The key empirical demonstrations of equivariance are somewhat contrived: the graph-level test set is rotated by a fixed 90 degrees, and non-equivariant baselines fail by construction in this setup; the node-level test rotation uses rejection sampling of 90-160 degree rotations. A broader distribution of rotations or data-augmentation baselines would strengthen the claims.

On the neural data benchmark, the improvement over MARBLE (0.66 vs 0.65 accuracy) is not statistically significant per the authors' own Wilcoxon test; the headline contribution there is speed and parameter count rather than performance. Notably, the comparison to CEBRA/LFADS is not apples-to-apples since those methods do not use vector-valued features, as the authors acknowledge.

Presentation has notable defects: several typos ('Guassian kernel', 'represtenta-tion', 'replaces with dyadic wavelets', Lemma A.2 misstates Q' as D x D), garbled notation in Section 2.3 (invariance equations render as x^(l) = x^(l)), and footnote 4 announcing code availability with what appears to be a missing/empty URL, which weakens reproducibility as submitted.

The relationship and empirical comparison between the theoretical dyadic VDWs of Section 3 and the actually-implemented non-dyadic InfoGain-selected wavelets with Dirac auxiliary signals (Appendix E.1) creates a gap between the analyzed object and the deployed object; the authors assert the theory extends readily but provide no formal statement for the modified version.

There is no explicit limitations section; limitations (e.g., requirement of ni >= D neighbors, sensitivity of local SVD to noise/degree constraints, non-uniqueness beyond sign flips when singular values are close) are either buried in footnotes or not discussed.
